# The External Correspondence Pack

*Thirteen letters for dealing with outside government. Prepared for the Founder
and for any officer authorised to write in the Kingdom's name to a police
department, a town hall, a state agency, or a legislative office.*

## How to use this pack

`government-correspondence` gives the general form of a letter to a public body
and `connecticut-foia-request` gives the records request. Read both once before
using anything here. This pack is the working set: the thirteen letters that
actually get sent, in the order a new institution usually needs them, each one
drafted to the same spine so that a body receiving three of them over two years
recognises the same organisation writing.

The pack assumes what `01-LEGAL-POSTURE` and `04-GOVERNMENT-RELATIONS-PROTOCOL`
establish and does not restate it. The short version, because it governs every
line below: the Kingdom's leverage is its status as a religious society and
charitable body, the First Amendment doctrines that protect internal religious
governance, RLUIPA against municipalities, RFRA against federal action, the
ministerial exception, consent-based arbitration, and the political weight of a
congregation whose members vote in the ward. None of that requires anyone to
concede anything about sovereignty, and every one of those instruments is
destroyed by asserting it.

### The spine every letter carries

Eleven elements. A letter missing any of them is a letter that can be set aside
without consequence, and public offices set aside what they can.

1. A reference number from the register in which the matter is recorded, in a
   form the recipient can quote back. Print the number and leave the register's
   internal prefix off the page where an outside reader could decode it into a
   claim. A reference block reading "G2G-0041" says government-to-government to
   anyone who pauses over it, and the closing section of this file explains why
   that phrase must never reach a town hall.
2. The date, written out.
3. The method of delivery, stated at the top, so the file shows how it went.
4. A recipient block naming an individual, with the correct title.
5. A subject line a clerk can route without reading the letter.
6. A first paragraph identifying who is writing, for what body, in what capacity.
7. A specific and lawful request, in the first or second paragraph.
8. The authority obliging or supporting the response, cited by section where one
   exists — and no citation where one does not, because a request dressed in a
   fake authority is worse than a request made as a courtesy.
9. A date by which a reply is sought, framed as what the Kingdom will do next.
10. A signature block with a name, an office, a return address, a telephone
    number, and an email address.
11. An enclosure list and a cc line, or the deliberate omission of both.

### Before any of these goes out

- [ ] **A record is open** in the Government-to-Government Contact Register, and
      the letter carries its reference in the form element 1 above requires — the
      digits, with the full internal number held in the register against them.
      The record is completed the day the letter is sent, not when a reply
      arrives. A records request opens instead in the Register of Public Records
      Requests, whose FOI prefix is unobjectionable and goes out as it stands.
      Anything addressed to a police department, a fire marshal, or an emergency
      service — letters 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 — opens in the Register of Public
      Safety and Emergency Services Liaison, which is the operating register for
      those dealings (`14-INTERFACING-WITH-OUTSIDE-GOVERNMENT` § 7). Where the
      underlying event is an incident it opens in the Register of Incidents
      first; where the letter forms part of a wider dealing with the same body it
      is linked to the contact register rather than entered twice.
- [ ] **The name, title, and address are verified this week** from the body's own
      website or by telephone.
- [ ] **The letterhead is plain.** No seal larger than the text, no device
      resembling a badge, shield, or the coat of arms of a government, no office
      name imitating a public agency. `04-GOVERNMENT-RELATIONS-PROTOCOL` § 4.
- [ ] **The signing officer's style is the external one.** Within the Kingdom the
      Founder is properly styled the Sovereign. On a letter to a records officer,
      "[Name], Founder and Presiding Officer, Apex Kingdom" is read and answered.
- [ ] **The entity name is accurate.** Do not sign to a public body as "Apex
      Tactical Corporation" unless that name is in fact an incorporated entity or
      a trade name recorded with the town clerk under Conn. Gen. Stat. § 35-1. A
      name asserting a corporate form the Kingdom does not hold is exactly the
      small inaccuracy a municipal attorney notices and keeps. Separately, and
      whatever that name's legal position turns out to be: the word "Tactical"
      does not go on paper sent to a police department, a fire marshal, or a
      school. To that reader it does not read as the name of a records office. It
      reads as equipment and organisation, it sits badly beside any mention of
      stewards in vests, and it is the one word in the Kingdom's vocabulary
      capable of turning a complainant into a subject. Correspondence with public
      bodies is signed for Apex Kingdom.
- [ ] **The letter has been read once against the closing section of this file**,
      "What never goes out over the Kingdom's name."
- [ ] **A follow-up date is in the calendar** and an officer is assigned to make
      the call.

### The letterhead

```
APEX KINGDOM
[OFFICE — e.g., OFFICE OF THE FOUNDER AND PRESIDING OFFICER]
[STREET ADDRESS]
Bridgeport, Connecticut [ZIP]
Telephone [NUMBER] · [EMAIL ADDRESS]
```

### Forms of address, and the Connecticut facts behind them

Every letter in this pack carries a `[SALUTATION]`, and getting it wrong is the
cheapest way there is to lose a reader. The address block is where an unfamiliar
organisation is first judged, and a title wrong by one word tells the recipient
that nothing else in the envelope was checked either. Verify the name and the
style from the body's own website in the week the letter goes out, and use the
style the officeholder uses about themselves.

The particulars that most often catch a writer working from another state's
template, each of which is noticed here immediately:

**There is no county government.** Connecticut abolished it in 1960. The counties
survive as lines on a map and as the names of judicial districts; there is no
county executive, no county council, and nothing to write to. Regional business is
done by councils of governments, which are voluntary associations of member
municipalities and hold no authority over a private organisation.

**There are no sheriffs.** The county sheriff system was abolished by
constitutional amendment in 2000. Civil process is served by state marshals, who
are appointed and are not police officers; courthouse and prisoner duties belong
to judicial marshals.

**Prosecutors are State's Attorneys.** The Division of Criminal Justice is headed
by the Chief State's Attorney, and each judicial district has a State's Attorney.
There is no District Attorney in Connecticut.

**The chief executive of a municipality is often not a mayor.** Cities take a
mayor. Towns on the selectman form take a first selectman, and where the incumbent
uses First Selectwoman that is the style to use. Towns on the
council-manager form are run by an appointed town manager or town administrator,
and the mayor, where there is one, chairs the council and does not run the town —
so a letter about an operational matter addressed to that mayor goes to the wrong
desk and costs a fortnight. Connecticut also has boroughs, whose chief executive
is a warden sitting with a board of burgesses.

**"The Honorable" belongs to the elected.** Mayors, first selectmen, legislators,
and judges take it in the address block, with the office in the salutation — "Dear
Mayor ——", "Dear First Selectman ——", "Dear Senator ——". Appointed officers,
including town managers, chiefs of police, fire marshals, assessors, and records
officers, take their actual title and no honorific. Applying it to an appointed
professional is a small error and it reads as flattery.

**Many towns have no police department.** They are policed by the Connecticut
State Police from a troop, in many cases with a resident trooper stationed in the
town under the arrangement authorised in Title 29 of the General Statutes; confirm
the section against the current General Statutes before citing it. Letters 4, 6,
and 8 in this pack are addressed to a chief of police who in those towns does not
exist. There the correspondence goes to the troop commander and the resident
trooper, and the town's own contact is the first selectman's office. Establish
which arrangement applies before drafting.

**It is the Secretary of the State**, not the Secretary of State. And some
municipalities, Bridgeport among them, maintain both a town clerk and a city clerk
holding different records. Confirm which office holds the record you want before
writing to either; a misdirected request is forwarded slowly, if at all.

# 1. Statement of institutional standing

## When to use this

Send this to any body that has never dealt with the Kingdom before, at the
beginning of the relationship rather than in the middle of a dispute. It goes to
a police department before there is an incident, to a town hall before there is
an application, to a legislative office before there is a problem, and to a state
agency before a grant round opens.

**This is the single highest-leverage document in the pack, and it is the one
most often skipped.** The reason is worth stating plainly. Every unfamiliar
organisation writing to a public office is triaged in the first thirty seconds
against a small number of questions the reader has learned to ask: is this a real
institution, does it have a lawyer, is it insured, is it a tax-exempt body or
somebody's private venture, who is actually in charge, and — the question the
reader will not write down — is this one of *those* letters. An organisation that
answers all six on one page, unprompted and before anything is at stake, is
placed in a different category permanently, and everything it sends afterwards is
read from inside that category. An organisation that answers none of them spends
two years being answered slowly.

The paragraph that does most of the work is the one stating what the Kingdom does
*not* claim. That is not a concession and it is not defensive. It is the fastest
available way to be removed from a file the recipient's counsel maintains, and to
be treated as what the Kingdom actually is.

## What must accompany it

A certified extract of the Charter rather than the whole of it; the Official
Citation of the Connecticut General Assembly of 5 October 2025, described exactly
as it is; a certificate of insurance; proof of tax status in whatever form the
Kingdom holds it; and the public verification address of the register. Nothing
else. Do not enclose a history, a manifesto, a seal sheet, or photographs.

Assemble for the reader rather than sending everything to everybody.
`docs/15-THE-STANDING-PACKET.md` § 5 sets out worked variants, and the police
variant in particular omits the Citation, the tax status, and the EIN — the first
because it bears on nothing that reader is deciding, the others because nothing
financial belongs in that envelope. Where a variant omits an item, cut both the
corresponding section of the letter and the numbered enclosure list to match. The
two must agree exactly, because the first thing a careful reader does with a
numbered list is count against it.

The extract rather than the Charter, because the reader will read what is
enclosed. An extract limited to the name, the purposes, the governance structure,
and the officers answers every question a public office actually has. The whole
Charter is a religious constitution written for the Kingdom's own members in the
Kingdom's own vocabulary, and one page of it read cold by a town attorney will
undo the careful paragraph on page one of the letter. Offer the full document on
request and provide it the same week if it is asked for — refusing would be worse
than enclosing it — but do not volunteer it.

For the same reason the letter gives the Charter's founding date in plain
English. *Nunc pro tunc* is a court's phrase for what a court does, and a private
body using it about its own instrument reads as an attempt to give that instrument
retroactive legal effect. The fact is unremarkable and survives translation:
the community dates itself from 30 October 2010 and wrote that down in 2025.

```
[CONGREGATION]. — OMIT THIS SENTENCE ENTIRELY IF THERE IS NO

[WHERE THE KINGDOM HAS INCORPORATED, STATE IT EXACTLY: It is

                                  [ADDRESS], [TELEPHONE]

                                  IF THE KINGDOM HAS NO REGISTERED

                                  NOT AGREED TO ACT]
  Postal address for service      [ADDRESS]

TAX STATUS AND INSURANCE

[THE TAX PARAGRAPH IS OMITTED FOR A POLICE DEPARTMENT, WHICH IS
 DECIDING NOTHING THAT TURNS ON IT; THE INSURANCE PARAGRAPH STAYS.
 STATE ONLY WHAT IS TRUE AND DOCUMENTED. EXAMPLES:
 "The Kingdom holds Employer Identification Number [NUMBER]. As a
 church it is exempt from federal income tax under 26 U.S.C.
 § 501(c)(3) and is excepted by 26 U.S.C. § 508(c)(1)(A) from the

 OR "The Kingdom holds a determination letter dated [DATE], a copy of
 which is enclosed."
 ADD WHERE APPLICABLE: "It is registered with the Department of
 Consumer Protection under the Solicitation of Charitable Funds Act,
 Conn. Gen. Stat. § 21a-190a et seq. / It claims the exemption
 available under that Act."]

The Kingdom carries general liability insurance with [INSURER],
policy [NUMBER], limits [AMOUNT], and directors and officers
liability with [INSURER], policy [NUMBER]. A certificate is
enclosed, and your office can be added as a certificate holder on
request.

RECORDS AND VERIFICATION

The Kingdom maintains a tamper-evident register of its instruments,
offices, property, and correspondence. Any document it issues carries
a reference number and a cryptographic digest that can be checked
against the published ledger at [PUBLIC VERIFICATION ADDRESS]. If you
ever receive a document said to come from the Kingdom and want to know
whether it is genuine, that address will tell you, and so will a
telephone call to the liaison named above.

RECOGNITION

[OMIT THIS WHOLE SECTION, AND ENCLOSURE 2 WITH IT, WHERE THE CITATION
 BEARS ON NOTHING THE READER IS DECIDING — A POLICE DEPARTMENT ABOVE
 ALL, WHERE IT READS AS STATUS-SEEKING TO PRECISELY THE AUDIENCE
 TRAINED TO NOTICE IT. THE SENTENCES BELOW ARE THE STANDARD
 DESCRIPTION AND ARE USED VERBATIM WHEREVER THE CITATION IS DESCRIBED
 OR REPRODUCED; DO NOT REWORD THEM.]

The Official Citation of the Connecticut General Assembly of
5 October 2025, introduced by nine legislators and signed by the
President Pro Tempore, the Speaker of the House, and the Secretary of
the State, is a ceremonial honour recognising Apex Kingdom's
contribution to cultural heritage, civic education, and community
empowerment. It confers no legal status, is not state recognition of a
tribe, and creates no government-to-government relationship. A copy is
enclosed, and I set the description out in the terms we use everywhere
so that there is no ambiguity about how we describe it.

WHAT THE KINGDOM DOES NOT CLAIM

The Kingdom is a private religious and charitable body. It claims no
sovereign status, no immunity from the process of any court, no
jurisdiction over any person who has not agreed to it in writing, and
no law-enforcement authority of any kind. Its officers hold no
peace-officer powers, carry no badge or credential suggesting
otherwise, and hold themselves out as none. Its internal tribunal
decides questions of faith, discipline, and governance among its own
members and nothing else; where a determination is to have effect
outside the membership it does so only as ordinary arbitration, on
written consent given in advance, under 9 U.S.C. § 2.

I set this out unprompted because it is a fair thing for a public
office to have in mind when a body called a Kingdom writes to it, and
it is better answered here than left open.

I would welcome the chance to introduce myself in person at your
convenience, and I will telephone your office in the week of [DATE] to
ask whether that would be useful. In the meantime nothing is required
of you, and I am grateful for your time.

Respectfully,

[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[STREET ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]

Enclosures:  1. Certified extract of the Charter of Apex Kingdom
                [the full Charter provided on request]

                Assembly, 5 October 2025 [OMIT AND RENUMBER WHERE
                THE RECOGNITION SECTION IS OMITTED]
             3. Certificate of insurance
             4. [Determination letter / Certificate of
                incorporation / Trade name certificate — LIST ONLY
                WHAT IS ACTUALLY ENCLOSED]

cc:          [NONE. Counsel is named in the body above, and copying
             counsel on an introduction signals the dispute this
             letter exists to precede — more loudly than certified
             mail would. If the relationship is already adverse
             enough to want counsel on the cc line, this is the
             wrong letter.]
```

## Delivery, and what to do with the answer

Send by email and by ordinary first-class mail. Certified mail is wrong here: it
signals a dispute where there is none, and this letter's entire purpose is to
arrive before any dispute exists.

Most recipients will not reply, and that is not a failure. The letter's value is
that it is in the file. Record it in the contact register as sent, mark the
response as outstanding, and set the follow-up call for the date named — then
make the call, because a call to a body that has your standing statement in front
of it is a different call.

Where a reply comes, note the name of whoever signed it; that is now the
Kingdom's route into that office. Where the reply asks a question about status,
answer it in writing the same week, plainly, and update this letter for the next
recipient. Refresh the whole statement annually, or immediately on any change of
officers, counsel, insurance, or address, and send the refreshed version to every
body that holds the old one. An out-of-date standing statement in a police
department's file is worse than none.

# 2. Designation of liaison

## When to use this

Send it once the relationship exists, either with the standing statement or
shortly after it, and again whenever the officer changes. Its function is
mundane and its value is high: it means the body always knows who to telephone,
and it means the Kingdom always knows who was told what.

It also does quiet defensive work. Where every dealing runs through a named
liaison, a later claim that some member or supporter said something on the
Kingdom's behalf is answerable from the file rather than from memory.

## What must accompany it

Nothing, unless the standing statement has not gone out, in which case send both
together and lead with the standing statement.

## Delivery, and what to do with the answer

Email and first-class mail. No reply is expected.

Two disciplines make the designation worth anything. First, the hours stated must
be hours the telephone is actually answered; a liaison line that rings out
teaches the office to route around the Kingdom, and it will not route back.
Second, when the officer changes, this letter goes out again the same week to
every body holding the old one, and the old officer stops answering. A liaison
who has left and is still fielding calls is how an organisation ends up bound by
something nobody authorised.

# 3. Notice of representation by counsel

## When to use this

Send it when a matter has become adverse — a claim threatened or made, an
investigation opened, an enforcement action begun, a denial the Kingdom intends
to challenge — and counsel has been engaged for that matter. Send it the day
counsel is engaged.

The letter does two things. It routes further communication to a lawyer, which
protects officers from saying something in an unguarded telephone call that
becomes the government's best evidence. And it signals, without a word of
threat, that the Kingdom is not going to be handled informally. Both effects are
worth having; neither survives the letter being sent too early. A notice of
representation on a routine permit question converts a clerk into an adversary
and doubles the time everything takes.

Note the limit honestly: naming counsel does not bar a government from contacting
the Kingdom's officers in every context. Rules restricting a lawyer's
communications with a represented party bind lawyers, and a police officer
conducting a criminal investigation is not a lawyer. What the letter does is put
the request on the record and give the Kingdom's counsel a clean objection if it
is ignored.

## What must accompany it

Nothing. This letter is short by design. Do not attach the merits.

```

Re:  [THE MATTER, IN ONE LINE, WITH THE BODY'S OWN FILE NUMBER — e.g.,

Dear [SALUTATION]:

I write on behalf of Apex Kingdom, a religious society and charitable

The Kingdom has engaged counsel in this matter:

This letter is not a refusal to cooperate and should not be read as
```

## Delivery, and what to do with the answer

Certified mail with return receipt, and email. The date of receipt matters here
in a way it does not in most of this pack, because a later argument about whether
the body knew the Kingdom was represented turns on it. Record the article number
in the Register of Notices and Proof of Service.

From the moment this goes out, three rules bind every officer of the Kingdom.
Nobody discusses the matter with the body except through counsel. Nobody
discusses it in writing anywhere — including internally on channels that are not
privileged — without asking counsel first. And the internal litigation hold
issues immediately, per `05-EVIDENCE-AND-CHAIN-OF-CUSTODY`; deletion that would
have been innocent last month is not innocent now.

If the body contacts an officer directly after this letter, the officer says that
the Kingdom is represented, gives counsel's number, ends the conversation
courteously, and writes a note of it the same hour. The officer does not argue
about whether the contact was proper. That is counsel's argument to make later,
and it is a better one if the officer did not make it first.

# 4. Report of a crime or incident to a police department

## When to use this

Use it as a complainant, when the Kingdom, its property, its premises, or its
members have been the victim of a crime or of conduct the police should know
about. Use it after the emergency call, not instead of it: where anything is in
progress or anyone is at risk, the telephone call comes first and this letter
follows.

Use it also where an incident has already been reported by telephone and the
Kingdom wants a written, dated account in the department's file. Departments lose
verbal reports. A one-page written complaint with a date on it does not
disappear, and it is the document that makes a later pattern provable.

**Understand what this letter does not do.** In most departments a letter does
not open a case. A report is taken by an officer, at the scene, at the station,
or over the telephone, and the case number comes from that. A complaint posted to
a chief's office with nothing behind it is logged as correspondence and routed for
information, and the writer discovers six weeks later that no case exists and that
the evidence has aged. So either send this after a report has been taken,
referring to it by case number, or send it and telephone the desk the same day to
ask that an officer take the report. The letter is the record that supports the
report; it is not a substitute for making one.

**The single most important discipline here is accuracy.** Write only what the
Kingdom saw, and mark plainly what it was told by someone else and by whom.
Making a false written statement and falsely reporting an incident are themselves
crimes in Connecticut — the false-statement offence sits at Conn. Gen. Stat.
§ 53a-157b and the false-reporting offences in the same title, and the current
section numbers should be confirmed against the General Statutes before any of
them is referred to in writing. Beyond the criminal exposure there is a practical
point that matters more: one overstated sentence in a first complaint is what a
department will remember about the Kingdom for a decade.

The second discipline is jurisdictional and it is not negotiable. Reporting means
the matter now belongs to the police and to the State's Attorney. The Kingdom
does not investigate in parallel, does not interview suspects, does not
"secure" anything beyond its own premises, and sends nobody in anything
resembling a uniform. `01-LEGAL-POSTURE` § 4 is the boundary and it does not move
because an incident was upsetting.

## What must accompany it

A record already open in the Register of Incidents, with its number on the
letter. Photographs, video, or documentary exhibits listed and provided as copies
— never originals, which stay in the Evidence Vault with the chain of custody
recorded per `05-EVIDENCE-AND-CHAIN-OF-CUSTODY`. Where the department wants
originals it will say so, and they are handed over against a receipt.

## The letter

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD]

[DATE]

BY EMAIL TO [ADDRESS] AND BY HAND AT THE RECORDS WINDOW

[FULL NAME]
[Chief of Police / Commanding Officer, [DISTRICT] / Detective
 Bureau — ADDRESS IT TO A NAMED PERSON WHERE ONE IS KNOWN]
[NAME] Police Department
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY], Connecticut [ZIP]

Re:  Complaint of [OFFENCE OR CONDUCT, PLAINLY — e.g., "criminal
     mischief and trespass at 000 Main Street"]
     Date of occurrence: [DATE AND TIME]
     [Department case number: [NUMBER], where one has been issued]
     Our reference: [INC RECORD NUMBER]

Dear [SALUTATION]:

I am [FULL NAME], [OFFICE HELD] of Apex Kingdom, a religious society
and charitable trust operating in [BRIDGEPORT]. I write as complainant
on behalf of the Kingdom to report the matter set out below and to ask
that it be recorded and investigated.

1. WHAT HAPPENED

   On [DATE] at approximately [TIME], at [FULL ADDRESS], [SET OUT THE
   FACTS IN SHORT NUMBERED SENTENCES, IN ORDER, IN PLAIN LANGUAGE.
   STATE ONLY WHAT IS KNOWN. WHERE SOMETHING WAS REPORTED BY ANOTHER
   PERSON, SAY SO AND NAME THEM: "[NAME] told me that ...". DO NOT
   CHARACTERISE, DO NOT SPECULATE ABOUT MOTIVE UNLESS THERE IS
   EVIDENCE OF IT, AND DO NOT NAME A SUSPECT UNLESS THERE IS A BASIS
   FOR DOING SO.]

2. HARM AND LOSS

   [WHAT WAS DAMAGED, TAKEN, OR INJURED, WITH ESTIMATED VALUE WHERE
   IT CAN BE ESTIMATED HONESTLY, AND WHETHER ANYONE WAS HURT.]

3. WITNESSES

   [NAME], [RELATIONSHIP TO THE KINGDOM], [TELEPHONE] — [ONE LINE ON
   WHAT THEY SAW]. [EACH WITNESS HAS BEEN ASKED BEFORE BEING NAMED
   AND HAS AGREED TO BE CONTACTED.]

4. EVIDENCE HELD

   [LIST — e.g., "Photographs of the damage taken on [DATE] (copies
   enclosed, 6 images); video from the camera at the [LOCATION]
   covering [TIME] to [TIME] (available on request in native format);
   the note left at the door (original retained; photograph
   enclosed)."]

   The originals are held at [LOCATION] and will be produced to your
   department on request. Our camera system overwrites after
   [NUMBER] days, and the footage covering this period has been
   copied and preserved.

5. WHAT IS ASKED

   I ask that this complaint be recorded, that a case number be
   issued to me, and that the matter be assigned for investigation. I
   would be grateful if you would tell me the case number and the
   name of the assigned officer.

   [WHERE RELEVANT: I also ask that the department consider [SPECIFIC
   AND MODEST — e.g., "collecting the footage from the business at
   000 Main Street, which faces the affected door"].]

The Kingdom will cooperate fully with any investigation. Its officers
and members are available for interview at your convenience, and I
will make premises and records available on request. I am willing to
give a signed written statement and will attend the station for that
purpose at any time convenient to your officers, and I will supply
whatever identifying details your report form requires. The Kingdom
wishes this complaint pursued and will cooperate with any
prosecution, including by attending court if required. We are not
conducting any inquiry of our own and will not do so.

Please direct any question about this complaint to me at the numbers
below, or to [LIAISON NAME] at [TELEPHONE], who is our contact for
your department. I will telephone the records unit on [DATE — ABOUT A
WEEK OUT] to confirm the case number if I have not received it before
then.

Thank you for your attention to this and for the work your officers
do in [NEIGHBOURHOOD].

Respectfully,

______________________________
[FULL NAME]
[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[STREET ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]

Enclosures:  1. Photographs, [NUMBER] images, taken [DATE]
             2. [OTHER EXHIBITS, LISTED AND NUMBERED]

cc:          [COUNSEL — ONLY WHERE THE INCIDENT MAY BECOME A CIVIL
             CLAIM OR AN INSURANCE MATTER; OTHERWISE OMIT]
```

## Delivery, and what to do with the answer

Deliver by hand at the records window and ask for the copy to be date-stamped;
that stamped copy is the proof the complaint was made and is worth the trip.
Follow with an email to the department's published address so there is an
electronic timestamp as well.

Record the case number in the incident record the day it is issued. Where no case
number comes within a week, telephone the records unit — not the chief — and ask
for it. Where a report exists but has not been provided, the next letter is
number 5 in this pack.

Where the department declines to take a report, do not argue at the counter. Ask
for the reason, write it down with the name and badge number of the person who
gave it, and put that fact in the incident record. It is a fact of some
consequence later, and it is worth more written down calmly than won at the
window.

Where an insurance claim will follow, the case number is usually a precondition
to the claim, so open the claim only once it exists.

---

# 5. Request for a copy of a police report

## When to use this

Use it to obtain the department's own report of an incident — one the Kingdom
reported, one in which a member was involved, or one bearing on a matter the
Kingdom is dealing with. Frame it as what it is: an ordinary request under the
Connecticut Freedom of Information Act, made by a private body with no more
authority than any resident has. That framing is why it works. It concedes
nothing, requires nobody's permission, and is routed to a records officer rather
than to whoever has been slow to return calls. Many Connecticut records divisions
are commanded by a sworn officer, so establish the rank before writing; "Dear
Lieutenant ——" where that is the rank is correct and tells the reader the writer
knows the department.

Read `connecticut-foia-request` first. This is that letter, cut down and pointed
at a police department, and the general notes there on specificity, fees, and the
appeal window all apply here without repetition.

Understand the two features that make police records different from other public
records. First, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-210(b)(3) exempts records of law enforcement
agencies, not otherwise available to the public, compiled in connection with the
detection or investigation of crime, within the categories that subdivision sets
out — the identity of informants, uncorroborated allegations, signed witness
statements, and others. An open investigation will therefore often produce a
lawful partial refusal, and that is not obstruction. Second, a separate provision
of the Act governs records of arrest, and the practical scope of what must be
released while a prosecution is pending has been litigated; the current text and
subsection should be confirmed against the General Statutes rather than asserted
from memory.

The four-business-day interval at Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-206(a) — within which a
denial of the right to inspect or copy must be made in writing, a failure to
comply being deemed a denial — is the statutory norm and it is worth citing. It
is not the only interval in that section, and the exception bites here more often
than anywhere else. Where a request is determined to reach records subject to
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-214(b) and (c) — an employee's personnel or medical file or
a similar file, which a request touching a named officer's conduct frequently is
— § 1-206(a) allows ten business days rather than four, and the department must
notify the officer and any collective bargaining representative, who may object
within the period § 1-214 gives them, after which the department cannot disclose
without an order of the Commission. That is a lawful delay and not an evasion,
and a letter that has already announced a four-day deadline reads badly against
it. Say four business days, and say it subject to that section.

Say plainly in the letter, too, that the department's own published records procedure
governs how a request is made and processed, and confirm the exact intervals and
the department's form against that procedure before relying on any of them. A
requester who quotes a deadline wrongly has handed the department a reason to
answer the deadline instead of the request.

Three further things a records officer notices. The four-day interval governs the
making of a denial; it is not a production deadline, and a requester who writes as
though the department must hand over a file within four business days is corrected
on that point rather than answered on the request. Fees for copies are capped by
Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-212, with different maxima for state and municipal agencies
and separate provision for records transmitted electronically; confirm the current
figures against the General Statutes before authorising an amount, because a
requester who has the cap right is dealt with as somebody who has done this
before. And the Act gives a right to existing records — it does not oblige an
agency to create a record, to compile one, or to answer questions. A request
phrased as a question is refused correctly and costs a month.

Where the request reaches body-worn or dashboard camera recordings, expect delay
and expect redaction. Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-6d governs police body-worn recording
equipment and what must be done with what it captures; confirm its current text
before relying on any part of it. The practical consequence is that this is the
slowest and most expensive part of any request, and it is better made narrowly —
the officers who actually responded, the period from dispatch to clearance — than
as a request for everything, which invites a fee estimate designed to end the
conversation.

## What must accompany it

A record open in the Register of Public Records Requests, with the statutory
response date computed the day the request goes out and the thirty-day appeal
window noted. Where the request concerns a matter the Kingdom reported, the
incident record number.

## The letter

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD]

[DATE]

BY EMAIL TO [ADDRESS] AND BY CERTIFIED MAIL

[FULL NAME]
[Records Officer / Records Division]
[NAME] Police Department
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY], Connecticut [ZIP]

Re:  Request for public records under the Freedom of Information Act,
     Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-200 et seq.
     Case number [NUMBER], incident of [DATE] at [LOCATION]
     Our reference: [FOI RECORD NUMBER]

Dear [MR./MS. OR RANK] [SURNAME]:

This is a request to inspect and copy public records under the
Connecticut Freedom of Information Act, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-200 et
seq. It is made by Apex Kingdom, a religious society and charitable
trust operating in [BRIDGEPORT]. [WHERE APPLICABLE: The Kingdom was
the complainant in the matter below.]

1. RECORDS REQUESTED

   Concerning case number [NUMBER], reported [DATE], at [LOCATION]:

   (a) the incident or offence report and any supplemental or
       continuation reports;
   (b) the narrative and any officer's written statements;
   (c) the computer-aided dispatch record for the call, including
       times of dispatch, arrival, and clearance;
   (d) any photographs, sketches, or diagrams;
   (e) any body-worn or dashboard camera recording made by the
       officers who responded, covering the period from dispatch to
       clearance, in native format;
   (f) the property or evidence receipt for anything taken;
   (g) the disposition of the case as recorded to date; and
   (h) [ANY FURTHER CATEGORY, DESCRIBED SO A CLERK COULD FIND IT].

2. FORMAT AND FEES

   Please provide electronic records in native electronic format,
   with metadata intact, by email or on portable media, which is
   ordinarily less costly to the department than copying. I authorise
   fees up to [$25.00] without further approval and ask that you tell
   me the estimated cost before any charge beyond that is incurred,
   so that I may narrow the request if it would help.

3. EXEMPTIONS AND PARTIAL PRODUCTION

   I recognise that Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-210(b)(3) exempts certain
   records of law enforcement agencies compiled in connection with
   the detection or investigation of crime, and that other
   exemptions and the provisions of the Act governing records of
   arrest may apply. I am not asking for anything the department is
   obliged or entitled to withhold.

   Where a record is withheld in whole or in part, please produce the
   portions that are not exempt with only the exempt material
   redacted, identify what has been withheld by date, author, and
   general subject, and state in writing the subdivision of Conn.
   Gen. Stat. § 1-210(b) or other statute relied on for each
   withholding.

   Where a record is withheld because the investigation is open,
   please say so and, if you can, indicate when the position might be
   reviewed. I will re-request rather than press the point now.

4. RESPONSE

   Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-206(a) requires that a denial of the right to
   inspect or copy be made in writing within four business days of a
   request — ten business days where the request is determined to be
   subject to subsections (b) and (c) of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-214 —
   and provides that a failure to comply within the applicable period
   is deemed a denial. I understand that the department's own
   published records procedure governs how requests are made and
   handled, and I will follow it; if this request should be made on a
   departmental form or sent to a different address, please tell me
   and I will resubmit it the same day rather than have it sit.

   If narrowing this request would allow a faster or fuller response,
   please telephone or email me and I will work with you. I would
   much prefer to adjust the request than to receive a refusal for
   want of specificity. I will follow up by telephone on [DATE].

Thank you for your assistance.

Respectfully,

______________________________
[FULL NAME]
[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[STREET ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]

Enclosures:  [DEPARTMENTAL REQUEST FORM, WHERE ONE EXISTS AND HAS
             BEEN COMPLETED]
```

## Delivery, and what to do with the answer

Email and certified mail, and keep both proofs; the response period runs from the
request and a disputed transmission date costs the whole point.

When the response arrives, do three things the same day. Record what was produced
and what was withheld, with the exemption claimed for each withholding. Check
that every withholding actually names an exemption — a withholding with no
subdivision cited is not a lawful denial, and one courteous sentence saying so
produces the records more often than an appeal does. And compute the appeal date:
from a denial, actual or deemed, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 1-206(b)(1) allows thirty
days to file a notice of appeal with the Freedom of Information Commission. That
window is jurisdictional and nothing revives it — not a promise to look again,
not a late partial production, not an apology.

Where the refusal is because the investigation is open, diary the request to be
made again after disposition, and say nothing further. Pressing an open case is
how a complainant becomes a nuisance in a file that will be read later.

---

# 6. Report of a bias-motivated incident

## When to use this

Use it where an incident against the Kingdom, its premises, its symbols, or its
members appears to have been motivated in whole or in part by religion, race,
ethnicity, national origin, or another protected characteristic, and the Kingdom
wants that motivation recorded rather than left to inference.

This letter exists because of a specific administrative fact. Whether an incident
is counted as a bias incident is a classification decision made by an officer
filling in a form, usually early, usually on thin information, and once made it
is rarely revisited. Connecticut agencies report to the state, and the state
reports into the federal Uniform Crime Reporting programme, now collected through
the National Incident-Based Reporting System. An incident not flagged at intake
is invisible in every count thereafter — which matters for the department's own
resource decisions, for state and federal grant eligibility, and for the
Kingdom's ability, three years from now, to show a pattern rather than an
anecdote.

Be careful and be honest. Ask that the bias element be *considered and recorded
if supported*; do not assert a motive the evidence does not carry. An
overstated bias report that the department cannot substantiate damages the next
one, which may be the one that matters.

The legal furniture, stated accurately. Connecticut's intimidation based on
bigotry or bias offences sit at Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 53a-181j, 53a-181k, and
53a-181l, with the associated definitions in the same run of sections; confirm
the degrees and current text before citing a particular one. Conn. Gen. Stat.
§ 46a-58 addresses deprivation of rights and includes conduct directed at
religious property, and the current subsection should likewise be confirmed.
Federally, 18 U.S.C. § 247 reaches intentional damage to religious real property
and obstruction of the free exercise of religious beliefs where its jurisdictional
elements are met, and 18 U.S.C. § 249 is the general hate-crime provision. Data
collection derives from the Hate Crime Statistics Act, which was enacted as a
note to 28 U.S.C. § 534 and has since been editorially reclassified into Title 34
of the United States Code; Connecticut's own requirement that the state police
collect data on crimes motivated by bigotry or bias sits in Title 29 of the
General Statutes. Confirm the current codification of both before either is cited
in a letter, and do not quote a section number from memory.

## What must accompany it

Everything that supports the bias element and nothing that does not: photographs
of graffiti or symbols before removal, the original of any note or message,
message headers where the contact was electronic, and a dated list of prior
incidents with their case numbers where a pattern is being asserted. Do not clean
or paint over anything before it has been photographed and the police have been
given the chance to see it.

## The letter

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD]

[DATE]

BY EMAIL TO [ADDRESS] AND BY HAND

[FULL NAME]
[Chief of Police / Commander, [DISTRICT] / Detective Bureau]
[NAME] Police Department
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY], Connecticut [ZIP]

Re:  Incident of [DATE] at [LOCATION] — request that the bias element
     be considered and recorded
     [Department case number: [NUMBER]]
     Our reference: [INC RECORD NUMBER]

Dear [SALUTATION]:

I am [FULL NAME], [OFFICE HELD] of Apex Kingdom, a religious society
and charitable trust operating in [BRIDGEPORT]. I write further to
[the complaint made on [DATE] / the report taken by Officer [NAME] on
[DATE]] to set out why the Kingdom believes the incident may have
been motivated by [religion / race / ethnicity / national origin /
[OTHER]], and to ask that the bias element be considered by the
assigned investigator and recorded in the report if it is supported.

1. THE FACTS SUPPORTING A BIAS ELEMENT

   [SET OUT ONLY WHAT IS EVIDENCE, IN SHORT NUMBERED SENTENCES —
   e.g., "(a) The words painted on the north door were '[QUOTE
   EXACTLY]'. (b) The only building on the block affected was the
   Kingdom's premises, and the two adjoining commercial premises,
   which have the same street exposure, were untouched. (c) The
   damage was to the [RELIGIOUS OBJECT OR SYMBOL] and to nothing
   else, although [ITEM OF VALUE] was within reach and was not
   taken."]

2. CONTEXT, IF ANY

   [PRIOR INCIDENTS, EACH WITH ITS DATE AND CASE NUMBER WHERE ONE
   WAS ISSUED. IF THERE ARE NONE, SAY SO: "The Kingdom has not
   previously reported an incident of this kind."]

3. WHAT IS ASKED

   (a) That the assigned investigator consider whether a bias
       motivation is supported by the evidence, and that the finding
       either way be recorded in the report.

   (b) That, if it is supported, the incident be classified as a bias
       incident for the department's reporting into the Uniform Crime
       Reporting programme and the National Incident-Based Reporting
       System, and reported onward as your procedures require.

   (c) That the department consider whether the conduct falls within
       Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 53a-181j to 53a-181l, or any other
       provision your officers judge applicable. I make no assertion
       about the correct charge; that is the department's judgment
       and the State's Attorney's, not mine.

   (d) That I be told the classification recorded, so that the
       Kingdom's own record is accurate.

I want to be clear that the Kingdom is not asking the department to
record a motive the evidence does not support. If the investigation
concludes that this was not bias-motivated, we would rather know that
and record it than have an incident counted that should not be. What
we ask is that the question be asked and answered rather than left
open.

The Kingdom will cooperate fully. Its officers and members are
available for interview, the physical evidence is preserved and
undisturbed, and we have not cleaned or repaired the affected area
pending your officers' attendance.

I will telephone [NAME OR THE DETECTIVE BUREAU] on [DATE] to ask about
the classification if I have not heard before then.

Thank you for your attention to this.

Respectfully,

______________________________
[FULL NAME]
[OFFICE HELD], Apex Kingdom
[STREET ADDRESS] · [TELEPHONE] · [EMAIL]

Enclosures:  1. Photographs, [NUMBER] images, taken [DATE], before
                any cleaning
             2. [THE NOTE / MESSAGE / SCREENSHOTS WITH HEADERS]
             3. Schedule of prior incidents with case numbers
                [WHERE THERE ARE ANY]

cc:          [COUNSEL, OR NOBODY. DO NOT COPY A CIVIL RIGHTS BODY,
             A PROSECUTOR, OR ANY OTHER AUTHORITY ON A FIRST REPORT.
             THE REASONS ARE BELOW, AND AN ESCALATION IS ITS OWN
             LETTER RATHER THAN A LINE ON THIS ONE.]
```

## Delivery, and what to do with the answer

By hand and by email, to the detective bureau or the assigned investigator rather
than to the chief's office, with a copy to the chief only where the matter is
serious or where an earlier report went nowhere.

On the cc line, resist the instinct. Copying a state or federal civil rights body
on a first report tells the department the Kingdom is building a complaint
against *it* rather than asking for help, and the cooperation the Kingdom needs
evaporates. Give the department a fair opportunity first. Where the pattern is
established, where reports have been made and nothing has been recorded, an
approach to the United States Attorney's Office for the District of Connecticut,
to the Office of the Chief State's Attorney, to the Connecticut Commission on
Human Rights and Opportunities, or to the Community Relations Service of the
United States Department of Justice — established by Title X of the Civil Rights
Act of 1964 to help resolve community conflict — is available and appropriate.
Confirm which unit within each handles matters of this kind before addressing
anything. That is a considered escalation, made in its own letter, not a cc
line on a first report.

Record the classification the department actually applies, whatever it is. A
maintained schedule of incidents, each with its date, case number, and recorded
classification, is the document that makes a pattern arguable years later, and
nothing else does.

# 7. Notice of a religious assembly or procession, and permit application cover

## When to use this

Use it whenever the Kingdom will gather outside its own premises, or in numbers
that affect a street, a park, a car park, or the neighbours — a procession, an
outdoor service, a vigil, a festival, a funeral cortege, a baptism at a public
waterfront.

Two things are happening in this letter and it is worth keeping them separate.
The first is a courtesy notice, sent because a police department that learns of
two hundred people on a street from the dispatcher is a department with a
problem, and one that learned of it three weeks earlier from a named liaison is a
partner. The second is a permit application cover, where the municipality's
ordinance requires a permit for the use in question.

Do not confuse the two, and do not use the first to avoid the second. A
municipality may lawfully require a permit for a parade or the use of public
streets and may impose reasonable regulation of time, place, and manner: *Cox v.
New Hampshire*, 312 U.S. 569 (1941); *Ward v. Rock Against Racism*, 491 U.S. 781
(1989). What it may not do is vest unbridled discretion in an official, and fee
and permitting schemes that turn on the content of the message or on an
official's estimate of hostile reaction have been struck down — *Forsyth County v.
Nationalist Movement*, 505 U.S. 123 (1992). Those are real protections and they
are asserted, if ever, from the position of an applicant who applied properly and
on time. An organisation that marched without applying has forfeited them.

The occupancy and fire questions belong to the local building official and fire
marshal under the State Building Code and the State Fire Safety Code adopted
under Title 29 of the General Statutes. Ask them which provisions they apply and
get the answer in writing; do not cite a code section to a fire marshal from
memory.

Three further things stop events that were otherwise applied for properly, and
all three are outside the office that grants the permit. Many Connecticut main
streets are state highways, and a municipality cannot authorise the closure or
occupation of one; that requires an encroachment permit from the Department of
Transportation under the provisions of Title 13a of the General Statutes, on the
Department's timetable rather than the town's — confirm the section against the
current General Statutes before citing it, and establish who owns the road before
choosing the route. Amplified sound is governed by the municipality's noise
ordinance, made under the noise control provisions of Title 22a; ask for the
ordinance rather than assume the permitted hours. And where food will be served
or sold, a temporary food event permit comes from the municipal health department
or the district health department covering the town, on its own form and with its
own lead time. A festival refused three days out has almost always been refused by
the health authority, not by the office that issued the permit.

## What must accompany it

The completed municipal application form, if there is one — find it before
writing, because a letter arriving without the form the office actually uses
starts a fortnight of correspondence. A certificate of insurance naming the
municipality as additional insured where required. A route map or site plan. The
name and number of the person in charge on the day.

A word on the people managing the event: call them **stewards**, or ushers, or
volunteers. Never marshals, never wardens, never anything with a rank. They wear
plain identifying clothing — a coloured sash, a lanyard, a printed vest saying
nothing but "steward" and the Kingdom's name — and nothing resembling a uniform,
badge, shield, or insignia. This is not fussiness; see the closing section.

## The letter

```
[APEX KINGDOM LETTERHEAD]

[DATE]

BY EMAIL TO [ADDRESS] AND BY FIRST-CLASS MAIL

[FULL NAME]
[Special Events Coordinator / Town Clerk / Chief of Police / Director
 of Public Facilities — WHOEVER THE ORDINANCE ACTUALLY NAMES]
[CITY OR TOWN] of [NAME]
[STREET ADDRESS]
[CITY], Connecticut [ZIP]

Re:  [Application for a [PARADE / SPECIAL EVENT / PARK USE] permit /
     Notice of a religious assembly] — [NAME OF THE EVENT],
     [DATE OF THE EVENT]
     Our reference: [OUR FILE NUMBER — DIGITS ONLY]

Dear [SALUTATION]:

I write on behalf of Apex Kingdom, a religious society and charitable
trust operating in [BRIDGEPORT], to [apply for a permit for / give
your office advance notice of] a religious [service / procession /
observance] to be held as follows.

  Event               [NAME AND ONE-LINE DESCRIPTION OF ITS
                      RELIGIOUS CHARACTER — e.g., "an annual
                      procession of witness, a religious observance
                      of the Kingdom"]
  Date and time       [DATE], assembling [TIME], concluding [TIME]
  Rain date           [DATE, OR "none — the observance proceeds in
                      any weather"]
  Place or route      [FULL DETAIL; ATTACH THE MAP. STATE WHETHER

                      certificate enclosed [naming the [CITY] as
                      additional insured, as your form requires]

The gathering is a religious observance of the Kingdom. I state that
as a fact for your record rather than as an argument, and I make no
```
